title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: "I lay on my straw but couldn't sleep. I thought over the day's events. What struck me most was the gentle manner of these people. I longed to join them but didn't dare. I remembered too well how the villagers had treated me and resolved, whatever I might eventually decide to do, to stay quietly in my hovel for now — watching and trying to understand what motivated their actions.
"The cottagers rose before dawn the next morning. The young woman arranged the cottage and prepared food. The young man left after the first meal.

"This day passed exactly like the one before. The young man worked constantly outdoors. The girl did various hard tasks inside. The old man, whom I soon realized was blind, spent his leisure playing his instrument or sitting in thought. Nothing could exceed the love and respect the younger cottagers showed their elderly companion. They performed every small act of affection and duty with gentleness, and he rewarded them with kind smiles.

"They weren't entirely happy. The young man and the girl often went aside and seemed to weep. I saw no cause for their unhappiness, but it affected me deeply. If such lovely people could be miserable, it was less surprising that I — an imperfect, solitary being — should be wretched. But why were these gentle creatures unhappy? They possessed a delightful house (it seemed so to my eyes) and every luxury. They had fire for warmth and delicious food when hungry. They were well dressed. And most importantly, they had each other's company, exchanging looks of love and kindness every day. What did their tears mean? Did they really express pain? At first I couldn't answer these questions, but careful observation over time explained many things that had initially puzzled me.

"After some time I discovered one cause of the family's distress: poverty, which they suffered severely. Their food consisted entirely of garden vegetables and milk from one cow, which gave very little in winter when the owners could barely feed it. The two younger ones, I believe, often went painfully hungry. Several times I saw them place food before the old man while keeping none for themselves.

"This act of kindness moved me greatly. I'd been stealing food from their supplies at night for myself. When I realized I was causing them pain, I stopped and lived on berries, nuts, and roots from the nearby woods.

"I also found another way to help them. I noticed the young man spent much of each day gathering firewood. During the night, I often took his tools — I quickly figured out how to use them — and brought home enough fuel to last several days.

"The first time I did this, the young woman was astonished to find a large pile of wood outside her door in the morning. She called out in surprise, and the young man joined her, equally amazed. I noticed with pleasure that he didn't go to the forest that day but spent it repairing the cottage and working in the garden.

"Gradually I made an even more important discovery. I found that these people had a way of communicating their thoughts and feelings through speech. I noticed that words sometimes brought pleasure or pain, smiles or sadness, to the listener. This was a godlike power, and I desperately wanted to learn it. But every attempt failed me. Their speech was rapid, and the words they used had no obvious connection to visible objects. I couldn't find any pattern. With great effort, however, after spending several months in my hovel, I managed to learn the names given to some of the most familiar things: _fire, milk, bread,_ and _wood._ I also learned the cottagers' names. The young man and woman each had several names, but the old man had only one: _father._ The girl was called _sister_ or _Agatha,_ and the young man _Felix, brother,_ or _son._ I can't describe the delight I felt when I learned what each of these sounds meant and could say them myself. I picked up other words too, without fully understanding them yet: _good, dearest, unhappy._

"I spent the winter this way. The cottagers' gentle manners and beauty made me grow deeply fond of them. When they were sad, I felt sad. When they were happy, I shared their joy. I saw few other people, and whenever a stranger entered the cottage, their rough manners only highlighted how much better my friends were. The old man often tried to cheer up his children, as he sometimes called them. He'd speak in a warm, encouraging tone that gave even me pleasure. Agatha listened respectfully, her eyes sometimes filling with tears she tried to hide. But after listening to her father's words, she usually seemed more cheerful. Felix was always the saddest of the three. Even to my untrained eye, he seemed to have suffered more deeply than the others. But although his face was more sorrowful, his voice was more cheerful than his sister's — especially when he spoke to the old man.

"I could list countless small examples that revealed these kind people's natures. Despite their poverty, Felix took pleasure in bringing his sister the first little white flower that appeared through the snow. Early in the morning, before she was up, he cleared the snow from her path to the dairy, drew water from the well, and brought wood from the shed — where, to his constant amazement, he always found the supply replenished by an invisible hand. During the day, I believe, he sometimes worked for a neighboring farmer, since he often went out and didn't return until dinner, yet brought no wood with him. At other times he worked in the garden, but since there was little to do in the cold months, he read aloud to the old man and to Agatha.

"This reading had confused me greatly at first. But gradually I realized he was making many of the same sounds when reading as when talking. I guessed he was finding signs for speech on paper and desperately wanted to understand them too. But how could I, when I didn't even understand the sounds the signs represented? I improved steadily in this science, though not enough to follow actual conversation. I applied my whole mind to the task. I could clearly see that, although I longed to reveal myself to the cottagers, I shouldn't attempt it until I'd mastered their language. If I could speak well, they might overlook my physical ugliness — a subject the constant contrast with their beauty had made painfully clear to me.

"I had admired my cottagers' graceful forms, their beauty and delicate features. But what horror I felt when I saw myself reflected in a clear pool! At first I recoiled, unable to believe it was really me in the mirror. When I finally accepted that I was indeed the monster I am, I was filled with the bitterest despair and shame. Alas! I didn't yet fully grasp the fatal effects of this miserable deformity.

"As the sun grew warmer and days grew longer, the snow vanished. I saw bare trees and black earth. From then on, Felix was busier, and the heartbreaking signs of approaching hunger disappeared. Their food, as I later learned, was coarse but nourishing and sufficient. New plants sprouted in the garden. The signs of comfort increased daily as the season advanced.

"The old man, leaning on his son's arm, walked at noon each day when it wasn't raining — that, I found, was what they called it when water poured from the sky. This happened frequently. But a strong wind would quickly dry the earth, and the season became far more pleasant.

"My life in the hovel followed a routine. In the morning I watched the cottagers. When they scattered to their various tasks, I slept. The rest of the day I spent observing my friends. When they went to bed, if there was moonlight or starlight, I went into the woods to collect my own food and fuel for the cottage. When necessary, I cleared their path and did the chores I'd seen Felix do. I later found out these labors, performed by an invisible hand, astonished them greatly. Once or twice I heard them use the words _good spirit_ and _wonderful,_ though I didn't yet know what those words meant.

"My thoughts grew more active. I longed to understand what drove these lovely people — why Felix seemed so sad and Agatha so sorrowful. I thought — foolish wretch! — that it might be in my power to restore their happiness. When I slept or was away, the images of the kind blind father, gentle Agatha, and excellent Felix appeared before me. I saw them as superior beings who would decide my destiny. In my imagination, I rehearsed a thousand versions of introducing myself to them, picturing their reactions. I imagined they'd be disgusted — until my gentle manner and kind words won first their favor, then their love.

"These thoughts energized me and drove me to study language with renewed passion. My voice was indeed harsh, but flexible. Though it was nothing like the soft music of their speech, I could pronounce the words I knew with reasonable ease. I was like the donkey compared to the lapdog in the fable — but surely the gentle donkey, whose intentions were kind despite his rough manners, deserved better than blows and curses.

"The pleasant spring rains and warm weather completely changed the look of the earth. People who had seemed to hide in caves during winter now scattered and busied themselves with farming. Birds sang more cheerfully. Leaves began to bud on the trees. Happy, happy earth! A fit home for gods — yet just a short time before, it had been bleak, damp, and inhospitable. My spirits rose with the beauty of nature. The past was wiped from my memory. The present was calm. The future glowed with bright rays of hope and the promise of joy."
